quizzes.passage:
The Jam Stall

Every Saturday, fifteen-year-old Lala helps her aunt Nargiz at a small stall in the town market. Her aunt makes jam from the fruit that grows in her garden: cherries in June, apricots in July and quinces in the autumn. At first, Lala only carried boxes and put the jars on the table. She was too shy to speak to customers, and when someone asked her a question, she always looked at her aunt for help.

One morning, Aunt Nargiz had to leave the stall for an hour to take a phone call. Lala was alone. An old man stopped and asked which jam was best for his grandchildren. quizzes.passage:
Why Do Cats Purr?

Anyone who has lived with a cat knows the soft, low sound it makes when it is relaxed: purring. For a long time, people believed that cats purr only when they are happy. Today we know that the truth is more complicated.

Scientists explain that purring is produced by the muscles in a cat's throat. These muscles move very quickly and make the air vibrate as the cat breathes in and out. That is why a cat can purr for a long time without stopping.

Cats do purr when they are comfortable, for example when they are lying on a warm sofa or being stroked. However, they also purr when they are frightened, hungry or even hurt. Mother cats purr to their kittens, and kittens begin to purr when they are only a few days old. This helps the kittens find their mother, because they cannot see well at that age.

Some researchers think that purring may also help cats relax and feel better when they are in pain. This idea has not been fully proven yet, and scientists are still studying it. One thing is certain: a purring cat is trying to communicate something, and a careful owner can learn to understand what it means.
quizzes.text: Why can a cat purr for a long time without stopping?
options: It purrs both when breathing in and out.
It does not need to breathe.
It stores air in its body.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «It purrs both when breathing in and out.».

quizzes.passage:
Bobik Comes Home

On a rainy evening in November, the Aliyev family's dog, Bobik, ran out of the garden gate and disappeared. Ten-year-old Murad had forgotten to close the gate after coming home from football practice. He felt terrible. The whole family went out with torches and called Bobik's name until midnight, but there was no sign of him.

The next morning, Murad's sister Aysu suggested making posters. Together they printed twenty posters with Bobik's photo and their phone number and put them up around the neighbourhood. Murad also wrote a message in a local online group. For two days nothing happened, and Murad began to lose hope.

On the third day, the phone rang. A woman who worked at a bakery three streets away said that a brown dog had been sleeping by the warm oven door every night. When the family arrived, Bobik jumped up and almost knocked Murad over. The baker laughed and said that Bobik had chosen the warmest place in town.

That evening, Murad fixed a small bell to the garden gate. 'Now I will always hear it,' he said. His father smiled and told him that everyone makes mistakes, but the important thing is to learn from them.
quizzes.text: Why did Bobik get out of the garden?
options: Murad forgot to close the gate.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «Murad forgot to close the gate.».

Ten-year-old Murad had forgotten to close the gate after coming home from football practice. He felt terrible. The whole family went out with torches and called Bobik's name until midnight, but there was no sign of him.

The next morning, Murad's sister Aysu suggested making posters. Together they printed twenty posters with Bobik's photo and their phone number and put them up around the neighbourhood. Murad also wrote a message in a local online group. For two days nothing happened, and Murad began to lose hope.

On the third day, the phone rang. A woman who worked at a bakery three streets away said that a brown dog had been sleeping by the warm oven door every night. When the family arrived, Bobik jumped up and almost knocked Murad over. The baker laughed and said that Bobik had chosen the warmest place in town.

That evening, Murad fixed a small bell to the garden gate. 'Now I will always hear it,' he said. His father smiled and told him that everyone makes mistakes, but the important thing is to learn from them.

quizzes.passage:
The Library Card

When Murad was eleven, his family moved to a new town, and for the first few weeks he did not know anyone. After school he usually sat in the kitchen and stared at his phone until his parents came home from work. His grandmother, who lived with them, did not say much about it. Instead, one rainy afternoon she took him by the hand and walked him to the public library two streets away.

Murad expected a quiet, boring room full of old books. What he found was a busy place: a group of children were building robots in one corner, and a man was teaching chess to three teenagers in another. The librarian, a tall woman with green glasses, gave him a library card and told him he could borrow up to five books at a time. 'But be careful,' she said with a smile. 'Once you start, it's hard to stop.'

She was right. Murad began with a book about volcanoes, then moved on to adventure stories. Within a month he had joined the chess group, and by the end of the year he was helping younger children with their moves. He still has that first library card, although it is now bent and faded. He keeps it in his wallet, not because he needs it, but because it reminds him of the day the town stopped feeling strange.
quizzes.text: Why did Murad spend his afternoons looking at his phone?
options: His parents did not allow him to go out.
He did not know anyone in the new town yet.
He was preparing for a chess competition.
He was waiting for a call from his old friends.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «He did not know anyone in the new town yet.».

quizzes.passage:
Honeybees and Their Dance

A honeybee colony can contain tens of thousands of bees, but only a small number of them, the foragers, leave the hive to collect food. When a forager finds a good field of flowers, she faces a problem: how can she tell the others where it is? Bees cannot speak, and inside the hive it is completely dark.

The answer is a special movement that scientists call the waggle dance. The forager runs forward in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then turns and returns to the starting point, and repeats the movement many times. The direction of the straight run shows the direction of the food compared with the position of the sun. The length of the waggle shows the distance: the longer the waggle, the farther away the flowers are.

Other bees do not watch the dance, because they cannot see in the dark. Instead, they follow the dancer closely and feel her movements with their antennae. They also smell the flowers on her body, which helps them recognise the right place when they arrive. If the food is very close to the hive, the forager performs a simpler 'round dance', which tells the others only that food is nearby, not in which direction.

The waggle dance was explained in the twentieth century by the Austrian scientist Karl von Frisch, who later received a Nobel Prize for his work. His discovery showed that even very small animals can share surprisingly exact information.

options: The other bees are too far away.

Bees cannot speak and the hive is dark inside.
Most bees in the colony are asleep.
Flowers change their position every day.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «Bees cannot speak and the hive is dark inside.».

quizzes.passage:
A Town Without Cars

Twenty years ago, the centre of the small town of Valverde was full of traffic. Cars filled every street, the air smelled of fuel, and parents were afraid to let their children walk to school. Many shops in the old square had closed, because people preferred to drive to the big supermarket outside the town.

Then the new mayor made a decision that many people thought was crazy: she closed the town centre to private cars. Delivery vans could enter only early in the morning, and buses, taxis and emergency vehicles were still allowed. At first, shop owners were furious. They were sure that without cars, nobody would come to buy anything.

The opposite happened. Once the streets became safe and quiet, people started to walk and cycle there. Cafés put tables outside, children played in the square again, and several new shops opened. Within five years, the number of people living in the centre had grown, and the level of air pollution had fallen sharply.

Not everyone is happy, however. Some older residents say it is now harder for them to visit relatives who live in the centre, and drivers complain that the roads around the town are busier than before. The town council is now discussing a free electric minibus to help those who cannot walk far.
quizzes.text: Why had many shops in the old square closed?
options: The rents in the square were too high.
The shop owners moved to another town.
Delivery vans could not reach them.
The mayor ordered them to close.
People preferred to shop at a supermarket outside the town.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «People preferred to shop at a supermarket outside the town.».

quizzes.passage:
The First Snow

Aysel had lived all her life in a warm coastal city where it almost never snowed. So when her father got a job in a mountain town in the north, she imagined winter as something from a film: soft white hills, hot chocolate and quiet evenings by the fire.

The reality was different. In November the temperature dropped below zero, and Aysel discovered that her thin jacket was useless. Her fingers hurt when she walked to school, and the first time she stepped on ice, she fell and dropped all her books into a puddle. Her new classmates laughed, and she went home in tears, promising herself she would never go outside again until spring.

The next morning there was a knock at the door. It was Elvin, a boy from her class, holding an old pair of boots. 'These were my sister's,' he said. 'They have special soles. You won't fall in these.' He also showed her how to walk on ice — with small steps and bent knees, 'like a penguin'.

By January Aysel had learned to ski a little, and she had built her first snowman with Elvin and his sister. When her cousin from the coast called and asked whether she missed the sea, Aysel thought for a moment. 'Sometimes,' she said. 'But I've found something here that I didn't know I was missing.'
quizzes.text: How did Aysel imagine winter before moving?
options: as the best time for swimming
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «as calm and beautiful».

quizzes.passage:
Why Teenagers Need More Sleep

Many parents complain that their teenage children stay up late and are impossible to wake in the morning. It is easy to think that teenagers are simply lazy, but scientists say the real reason is biological.

Our bodies have an internal clock that tells us when to feel sleepy. This clock is controlled partly by a hormone called melatonin, which the body releases when it gets dark. In teenagers, melatonin is released about one or two hours later than in children and adults. As a result, a fifteen-year-old may honestly not feel tired until eleven o'clock or even later.

At the same time, teenagers still need between eight and ten hours of sleep a night. If they fall asleep at midnight and have to get up at half past six for school, they lose several hours of sleep every night. Over a week, this 'sleep debt' can affect their memory, their mood and their ability to concentrate in class.

Bright screens make the problem worse, because the light from phones and computers can delay the release of melatonin even further. Doctors therefore advise teenagers to switch off devices at least an hour before bed. Some schools in different countries have also started lessons later in the morning, and early studies suggest that their students arrive more alert and miss fewer classes.
quizzes.text: According to scientists, why do teenagers stay up late?
options: They need less sleep than children.
Their bodies feel sleepy later than adults' bodies do.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «Their bodies feel sleepy later than adults' bodies do.».

quizzes.passage:
The Old Bridge

For more than a hundred years, a narrow stone bridge connected the two halves of the village of Kendli. Farmers drove their sheep across it, children ran over it on their way to school, and couples took photographs on it on their wedding day. But one spring, after heavy rain, part of the bridge collapsed into the river.

The regional government said it would build a new bridge, but not for at least three years. Meanwhile, people on the east side had to make a twelve-kilometre journey by road to reach the school and the clinic on the west side. Some families talked about leaving the village altogether.

Then a retired engineer named Rasim suggested a different solution. He had worked on bridges all his life, and after examining the damage, he believed the old bridge could be repaired with local stone and the villagers' own work. He drew detailed plans, and an official from the region checked and approved them. Every weekend that summer, dozens of volunteers carried stones, mixed cement and cooked meals for the workers.

The bridge reopened in October. It is not exactly the same as before — the new section is a slightly different colour — but nobody seems to mind. In fact, the villagers now call that section 'Rasim's part', and children like to stand on it and look down at the river, as if the bridge belongs to them a little more than it did before.
quizzes.text: What happened to the bridge?
options: It was destroyed by a flood of sheep.
It was replaced by a new bridge.
It was closed because it was too narrow.
It was damaged by a truck.
Part of it fell into the river after heavy rain.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «Part of it fell into the river after heavy rain.».

Farmers drove their sheep across it, children ran over it on their way to school, and couples took photographs on it on their wedding day. But one spring, after heavy rain, part of the bridge collapsed into the river.

The regional government said it would build a new bridge, but not for at least three years. Meanwhile, people on the east side had to make a twelve-kilometre journey by road to reach the school and the clinic on the west side. Some families talked about leaving the village altogether.

Then a retired engineer named Rasim suggested a different solution. He had worked on bridges all his life, and after examining the damage, he believed the old bridge could be repaired with local stone and the villagers' own work. He drew detailed plans, and an official from the region checked and approved them. Every weekend that summer, dozens of volunteers carried stones, mixed cement and cooked meals for the workers.

The bridge reopened in October. It is not exactly the same as before — the new section is a slightly different colour — but nobody seems to mind. In fact, the villagers now call that section 'Rasim's part', and children like to stand on it and look down at the river, as if the bridge belongs to them a little more than it did before.

options: The school was closed for three years.
Their houses were damaged by the river.
They could not afford the road tax.
The government refused to help them.
Reaching the school and clinic became very difficult.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «Reaching the school and clinic became very difficult.».

quizzes.passage:
Never Too Late

My mother, Gulnar, could not swim. As a child she had lived far from any river or sea, and later she was always too busy — first with her studies, then with work and three children. Every summer, when we went to the beach, she sat under an umbrella and watched us, telling us not to go too far.

When she turned forty-five, she surprised us all. 'I've signed up for swimming lessons,' she announced at dinner. My brother laughed, thinking it was a joke. It was not. Twice a week she went to the pool, where she was the oldest person in a class of ten-year-olds.

The first lessons were hard. She was afraid to put her face in the water, and she told us that the children swam past her 'like little fish'. Once she came home so tired and embarrassed that she said she would stop. But the next Tuesday, she packed her bag again. 'If those children can do it,' she said, 'so can I.'

Last August, at the same beach where she used to sit under the umbrella, my mother walked into the sea and swam fifty metres to a yellow buoy and back. We stood on the shore and cheered. She came out of the water, smiling and out of breath, and said the thing I remember most: 'I wasn't too old. I was just too scared to start.'
quizzes.text: Why had Gulnar never learned to swim as a child?
options: She lived far from any water.
Her parents did not allow it.
She had three children to look after.
There were no teachers in her town.
quizzes.explanation: Cavab mətnə əsaslanır: «She lived far from any water.».
